chapters.title: Go Out of This City
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 1

1And it came to pass, when the sons of Israel were taken captive by the king of the Chaldeans, that God spoke to Jeremiah, saying, "Jeremiah, My chosen one, get up and go out of this city, you and Baruch, for I am going to destroy it because of the multitude of the sins of those who live in it.

2For your prayers are like a firm pillar in the middle of it, and like an unbreakable wall around it.

3So now get up and go out, before the army of the Chaldeans surrounds it."

4Jeremiah answered, "I beg You, Lord, permit me, Your servant, to speak before You."

5The Lord said to him, "Speak, My chosen one Jeremiah."

6Jeremiah spoke, saying, "Lord Almighty, are You handing the chosen city over into the hands of the Chaldeans, so that the king may boast with the multitude of his people and say, 'I have prevailed over the holy city of God'?

7No, my Lord! But if it is Your will, let it be destroyed by Your own hands."

8The Lord said to Jeremiah, "Since you are My chosen one, get up and go out of this city, you and Baruch, for I am going to destroy it because of the multitude of the sins of those who live in it.

9For neither the king nor his army will be able to enter it unless I first open its gates.

10So get up and go to Baruch, and tell him these words.

11Get up at the sixth hour of the night, both of you, and come to the walls of the city, and I will show you that unless I first destroy the city, they cannot enter it."

12When the Lord had said this, He left Jeremiah.

Notes

  • v1 "when the sons of Israel were taken captive by the king of the Chaldeans" — the book is rendered from the Greek, and its verse numbers follow the Greek. The other witness is the Ge'ez, headed The Rest of the Words of Baruch; it has been read against the Greek for names, numbers and the shape of each passage, and the notes say where the two differ. The story is set on the night before Jerusalem falls.

  • vv1, 5, 8 "Jeremiah, My chosen one" — God's name for the prophet throughout the book. Twice in this chapter He gives the command to leave the city in the same words (vv1, 8), before and after Jeremiah's plea.

  • v2 "like a firm pillar in the middle of it, and like an unbreakable wall around it" — at Jeremiah's call God said, I Myself have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls against the whole land (Jeremiah 1:18). There the prophet stood against the city; here his prayers are its pillar and wall, and the city cannot fall while he is in it. Adamantinos, "unbreakable," is literally "of adamant."

  • vv6–7 "so that the king may boast… let it be destroyed by Your own hands" — Jeremiah does not ask that the city be spared. He asks that the Chaldeans not have the glory of taking it. Baruch's lament answers the same boast (4:8).

  • vv9, 11 "unless I first open its gates… unless I first destroy the city" — what Lamentations said no one believed, that foe or enemy could enter the gates of Jerusalem (Lamentations 4:12). In this book they do not: the city is opened from heaven before Babylon walks in (4:1–2).

  • v11 "the sixth hour of the night" — midnight, with the hours of the night counted from dusk. The Ge'ez has the same number here, at 2:9, and at 3:1, where the Greek says only the hour.

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

chapters.title: Tear Our Hearts
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 2

1Jeremiah ran and told these things to Baruch. When they went into the temple of God, Jeremiah tore his clothes, put dust on his head and went into the sanctuary of God.

2When Baruch saw him with dust sprinkled on his head and his clothes torn, he cried out with a loud voice, "Father Jeremiah, what is the matter with you? What sin has the people committed?"

3For whenever the people sinned, Jeremiah would sprinkle dust on his head and pray for the people until the sin was forgiven.

4Baruch asked him, "Father, what is this?"

5Jeremiah said to him, "Keep from tearing your clothes; rather, let us tear our hearts. Let us not draw water for the troughs, but let us weep and fill them with tears, for the Lord will not have mercy on this people."

6Baruch said, "Father Jeremiah, what has happened?"

7Jeremiah said, "God is handing the city over into the hands of the king of the Chaldeans, to take the people captive to Babylon."

8When Baruch heard this, he too tore his clothes, and said, "Father Jeremiah, who made this known to you?"

9Jeremiah said to him, "Wait with me a little while, until the sixth hour of the night, so that you may know that this word is true."

10So they both stayed at the altar weeping, with their clothes torn.

Notes

  • vv1–2 "tore his clothes, put dust on his head" — the signs of mourning, and in this book a signal Baruch knows: v3 explains that Jeremiah did it whenever the people sinned, and prayed until the sin was forgiven. Baruch reads the dust and asks only what the sin is. The Ge'ez begins the chapter in the temple, without the run to Baruch.

  • v2 "Father Jeremiah" — Baruch's name for him in every speech of the chapter. In the book of Jeremiah, Baruch is the scribe who writes at his dictation (Jeremiah 36:18); here he speaks to him as a son.

  • v5 "let us tear our hearts" — the call of Joel 2:13, to tear the heart and not the garment. Jeremiah turns it the other way: Joel called for it so that the LORD would relent, and Jeremiah says it in the same breath as the Lord will not have mercy on this people.

  • v5 "fill them with tears" — Jeremiah's own wish, Oh, that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears (Jeremiah 9:1), made into a picture: the troughs that hold water for the animals are to be filled by weeping.

  • v10 "they both stayed at the altar weeping" — thysiastērion, the altar. The two wait in the temple for the hour God named, and the next chapter opens at it.

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

chapters.title: The Vessels Given to the Earth
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 3

1When the hour of the night came, as the Lord had told Jeremiah, Jeremiah and Baruch went together to the walls of the city.

2There was a sound of trumpets, and angels came out of heaven holding torches in their hands, and they stood on the walls of the city.

3When Jeremiah and Baruch saw them, they wept, saying, "Now we know that the word is true."

4Jeremiah pleaded with the angels, saying, "I beg you, do not destroy the city yet, until I speak a word to the Lord."

5The Lord spoke to the angels, saying, "Do not destroy the city until I speak to My chosen one Jeremiah."

6Then Jeremiah spoke, saying, "I beg You, Lord, command me to speak before You."

7The Lord said, "Speak, My chosen one Jeremiah."

8Jeremiah said, "Now, Lord, we know that You are handing the city over into the hands of its enemies, and they will carry the people away to Babylon.

9What do You want me to do with the holy vessels of the service?"

10The Lord said to him, "Take them and give them over to the earth, saying, 'Hear, earth, the voice of the One who created you, who formed you in the abundance of the waters, who sealed you with seven seals for seven times; after this you will receive your beauty.

11Keep the vessels of the service until the gathering of the beloved.'"

12Jeremiah spoke, saying, "I beg You, Lord, show me what I should do for Abimelech the Ethiopian, for he has done many kindnesses to Your servant Jeremiah.

13He pulled me up out of the pit of mud. I do not want him to see the destruction of this city and its desolation; rather, have mercy on him, so that he may not grieve."

14The Lord said to Jeremiah, "Send him to the vineyard of Agrippa, and in the shadow of the mountain I will shelter him until I bring the people back to the city.

15But you, Jeremiah, go with your people to Babylon, and stay with them, bringing them good news until I bring them back to the city.

16But leave Baruch here until I speak with him."

17When the Lord had said this, He went up from Jeremiah into heaven.

18Jeremiah and Baruch went into the sanctuary, took up the vessels of the service and gave them over to the earth, as the Lord had told them.

19At once the earth swallowed them.

20The two of them sat down and wept.

21When morning came, Jeremiah sent Abimelech off, saying, "Take the basket and go to the estate of Agrippa by the mountain road, and bring back a few figs and give them to the sick among the people, for the joy of the Lord is on you, and glory is on your head."

22When Jeremiah had said this, he sent him away, and Abimelech went as he had told him.

Notes

  • vv1–2 "the walls of the city… angels came out of heaven holding torches" — the hour named in 1:11. The fire that takes Jerusalem is brought by angels, and they stand on the walls before any Chaldean does.

  • vv9–11, 18–19 "the holy vessels of the service… the earth swallowed them" — in the book of Jeremiah the vessels went to Babylon: They will be carried to Babylon, and there they will stay until the day I attend to them (Jeremiah 27:22), and the Chaldeans took what was of gold, in gold, and what was of silver, in silver (52:19). Here the holy vessels never leave the city. 2 Maccabees, which is not in this canon, tells a like story: Jeremiah hides the tent, the ark and the altar of incense in a cave, and the place is to stay unknown until God gathers His people together (2 Maccabees 2:4–8).

  • v11 "until the gathering of the beloved" — syneleusis, a coming together, a gathering. The beloved has no noun with it. In 4:7 the same word stands with one, the beloved people, and the gathering is then Israel brought back to the city, as vv14–15 promise twice. Read alone, the beloved can also be a person, and syneleusis his coming.

  • vv12–13 "Abimelech the Ethiopian… He pulled me up out of the pit of mud" — the man who drew Jeremiah out of the cistern, where there was no water in the cistern, only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud (Jeremiah 38:6). Jeremiah names him Ebed-melech the Cushite (38:7), and the Greek of Jeremiah Abdemelech the Ethiopian. This book calls him Abimelech, and the Ge'ez has the same name. God promised him, I will deliver you on that day (39:17); this chapter begins to keep it.

  • v14 "the vineyard of Agrippa" — a name of a later age: Agrippa is the name of the king in Acts (Acts 25:13), six centuries after Jeremiah. In v21 the place is the estate of Agrippa, reached by the mountain road.

  • v15 "bringing them good news" — euangelizomenos, the word of Isaiah's messenger, How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news (Isaiah 52:7). Jeremiah, sent so often with bad news, is sent to the exiles with good.

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

chapters.title: The Keys Thrown to the Sun
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 4

1When morning came, the army of the Chaldeans surrounded the city.

2The great angel blew the trumpet, saying, "Enter the city, army of the Chaldeans, for the gate has been opened for you.

3Let the king enter with his multitude, and let him take all the people captive."

4Jeremiah took the keys of the temple, went outside the city and threw them down before the sun, saying, "I say to you, sun: take the keys of the temple of God, and keep them until the day when the Lord asks you about them.

5For we have not been found worthy to keep them; we have become stewards of falsehood."

6While Jeremiah was still weeping for the people, they dragged him off with the people to Babylon.

7Baruch put dust on his head, sat down and wept this lament, saying, "Why has Jerusalem been laid waste? Because of the sins of the beloved people she was handed over into the hands of enemies, because of our sins and the people's.

8But do not let the lawless boast and say, 'We were strong enough to take the city of God by our own might.' It was because of our sins that she was handed over to you.

9Our God will have compassion on us and bring us back to our city; but you will have no life.

10Blessed are our fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, for they went out of this world and did not see the destruction of this city."

11When he had said this, Baruch went outside the city weeping and saying, "Grieving for you, Jerusalem, I have gone out from you."

12He stayed in a tomb, sitting there, and angels came to him and told him everything the Lord revealed to him through them.

Notes

  • vv1–3 "the gate has been opened for you… let the king enter" — God's word of 1:9, unless I first open its gates, kept. The Chaldeans are invited in by an angel; they do not break in.

  • vv4–5 "threw them down before the sun… we have become stewards of falsehood" — the keys are given to the sun to keep until the Lord asks for them, and Jeremiah says why: we have not been found worthy to keep them. He was of the priests who were in Anathoth (Jeremiah 1:1), and he speaks for all who held the temple. Epitropoi, "stewards," are those put in charge of what belongs to another.

  • v7 "Baruch put dust on his head, sat down and wept this lament" — the words of the line that opens the Greek of Lamentations: Jeremiah sat weeping, and lamented this lament over Jerusalem. Thrēnos, "lament," is that book's Greek name. Here it is Baruch who sits and laments, since Jeremiah has been taken away.

  • v7 "the beloved people" — the phrase that names the beloved of 3:11.

  • v8 "We were strong enough to take the city of God by our own might" — the boast Jeremiah feared in 1:6, I have prevailed over the holy city of God. Baruch answers it with the book's own account: the city fell to the sins of its people, not to the strength of Babylon.

  • v10 "Blessed are our fathers… they did not see the destruction of this city" — the dead are counted happy, as the Preacher counted them: So I praised the dead who are already dead more than the living who are still alive (Ecclesiastes 4:2). The fathers were spared the sight, as Abimelech is to be (3:13).

  • v12 "He stayed in a tomb" — mnēmeion, a burial place; the Ge'ez has a tomb too. Baruch, left behind in the ruined city, lives among the dead, and there the angels bring him word.

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

chapters.title: Sixty-Six Years Asleep
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 5

1Abimelech carried the figs in the heat of the day, and coming upon a tree, he sat down in its shade to rest a little.

2He leaned his head on the basket of figs and fell asleep, and he slept sixty-six years; he did not wake from his sleep.

3Afterward, when he got up from his sleep, he said, "I slept pleasantly for a little while, but my head is heavy, because I did not get enough sleep."

4Then he uncovered the basket of figs and found them dripping milk.

5He said, "I would like to sleep a little longer, because my head is heavy. But I am afraid that if I sleep I will be late waking, and Jeremiah my father will think poorly of me; for if he were not in a hurry, he would not have sent me out at dawn today.

6So I will get up and go on in the heat. Is there not heat and toil every day?"

7So he got up, lifted the basket of figs onto his shoulders and went into Jerusalem. He did not recognize it, not the house and not his own place, and he found none of his family and none of the people he knew.

8He said, "Blessed be the Lord, for a great trance has fallen on me today.

9This is not the city of Jerusalem. I have lost my way, because I came by the mountain road when I got up from my sleep; and because my head was heavy from not getting enough sleep, I have lost my way.

10It will be a wonder to tell Jeremiah that I lost my way."

11He went out of the city, and looking carefully he saw the landmarks of the city, and he said, "This is the city, yet I have lost my way."

12He went back into the city and searched, and found none of his own people, and he said, "Blessed be the Lord, for a great trance has fallen on me."

13Again he went outside the city, and stayed there grieving, not knowing where to go.

14He put down the basket, saying, "I will sit here until the Lord takes this trance away from me."

15As he sat, he saw an old man coming in from the field, and Abimelech said to him, "I say to you, old man: what city is this?"

16He said to him, "It is Jerusalem."

17Abimelech said to him, "Where is Jeremiah the priest, and Baruch the reader, and all the people of this city? I could not find them."

18The old man said to him, "Are you not from this city, that you remember Jeremiah today and ask about him after so long a time?

19Jeremiah is in Babylon with the people. They were taken captive by King Nebuchadnezzar, and Jeremiah is with them to bring them good news and to teach them the word."

20As soon as Abimelech heard this from the old man, he said, "If you were not an old man, and if a man were allowed to insult one older than himself, I would laugh at you and say you are mad, for saying, 'The people have been taken captive to Babylon.'

21Even if the lattices of the heavens had come down on them, there has not been time yet for them to go to Babylon.

22How long is it since my father Jeremiah sent me to the estate of Agrippa to bring a few figs to give to the sick among the people?

23I went and got them, and coming to a tree in the heat, I sat down to rest a little, leaned my head on the basket and fell asleep.

24When I woke, I uncovered the basket of figs, thinking I was late, and I found the figs dripping milk, just as they were when I gathered them.

25Yet you say the people have been taken captive to Babylon.

26So that you may know, take, look at the figs."

27He uncovered the basket of figs for the old man, and the old man saw them dripping milk.

28When he saw them, the old man said, "My son, you are a righteous man, and God did not want you to see the desolation of the city, so He brought this trance on you.

29Today it is sixty-six years since the people were taken captive to Babylon.

30So that you may learn, child, that what I tell you is true, look up at the field and see that the crops have not yet begun to grow.

31Look at the figs too: it is not their season. Then you will know."

32Then Abimelech cried out with a loud voice, "I will bless You, God of heaven and earth, the rest of the souls of the righteous in every place!"

33Then he said to the old man, "What month is this?"

34He said, "Nisan, that is, Aviv."

35Abimelech took some of the figs and gave them to the old man, and said to him, "God will light your way to the city above, Jerusalem."

Notes

  • vv2, 29 "he slept sixty-six years" — the number is the same in the Greek and the Ge'ez, here, at v29, and when Baruch and Jeremiah count the years (6:8; 7:28). God had promised to shelter him until I bring the people back to the city (3:14); he sleeps through the whole exile and wakes on the eve of the return.

  • vv8, 12, 14, 28 "a great trance has fallen on me… He brought this trance on you" — ekstasis, a state of being taken out of oneself. Abimelech uses it of his confusion; the old man sees what it was. The Greek of Genesis 2:21 has the same word for Adam's sleep: The LORD God made a deep sleep fall upon the human.

  • vv4, 24, 30–31 "dripping milk, just as they were when I gathered them… it is not their season" — the figs are as fresh as the hour they were gathered. The old man reads them as a sign: in Nisan no fig is in season and no crop is up, yet these were picked sixty-six years before and have not spoiled.

  • v17 "Baruch the reader" — anagnōstēs, the one who reads aloud, as Baruch did: Then Baruch read from the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the LORD (Jeremiah 36:10).

  • v21 "Even if the lattices of the heavens had come down on them" — hoi katarraktai tou ouranou, the words of the Greek of Genesis for the flood: the lattices of the heavens were opened (Genesis 7:11). Abimelech means that not even the flood could have moved a whole people to Babylon in one morning.

  • v34 "Nisan, that is, Aviv" — the month of the exodus, Today you are going out, in the month of Aviv (Exodus 13:4). The Ge'ez also names the day, the twelfth of the month.

  • v35 "the city above, Jerusalem" — the old man is blessed with the city that is not destroyed, the Jerusalem above, as Paul names it (Galatians 4:26).

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

As he sat, he saw an old man coming in from the field, and Abimelech said to him, "I say to you, old man: what city is this?"
He said to him, "It is Jerusalem."
Abimelech said to him, "Where is Jeremiah the priest, and Baruch the reader, and all the people of this city? I could not find them."
The old man said to him, "Are you not from this city, that you remember Jeremiah today and ask about him after so long a time?
Jeremiah is in Babylon with the people. They were taken captive by King Nebuchadnezzar, and Jeremiah is with them to bring them good news and to teach them the word."

As soon as Abimelech heard this from the old man, he said, "If you were not an old man, and if a man were allowed to insult one older than himself, I would laugh at you and say you are mad, for saying, 'The people have been taken captive to Babylon.'
Even if the lattices of the heavens had come down on them, there has not been time yet for them to go to Babylon.
How long is it since my father Jeremiah sent me to the estate of Agrippa to bring a few figs to give to the sick among the people?
I went and got them, and coming to a tree in the heat, I sat down to rest a little, leaned my head on the basket and fell asleep.
When I woke, I uncovered the basket of figs, thinking I was late, and I found the figs dripping milk, just as they were when I gathered them.
Yet you say the people have been taken captive to Babylon.
So that you may know, take, look at the figs."
He uncovered the basket of figs for the old man, and the old man saw them dripping milk.
When he saw them, the old man said, "My son, you are a righteous man, and God did not want you to see the desolation of the city, so He brought this trance on you.
Today it is sixty-six years since the people were taken captive to Babylon.
So that you may learn, child, that what I tell you is true, look up at the field and see that the crops have not yet begun to grow.
Look at the figs too: it is not their season. Then you will know."
Then Abimelech cried out with a loud voice, "I will bless You, God of heaven and earth, the rest of the souls of the righteous in every place!"
Then he said to the old man, "What month is this?"
He said, "Nisan, that is, Aviv."
Abimelech took some of the figs and gave them to the old man, and said to him, "God will light your way to the city above, Jerusalem."

chapters.title: The Basket of Figs
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 6

1After this Abimelech went outside the city and prayed to the Lord.

2An angel of the Lord came, took him by the right hand and brought him back to the place where Baruch was sitting, and he found him in a tomb.

3When they saw each other, they both wept and kissed each other.

4Baruch looked up and saw the figs covered over in Abimelech's basket.

5He lifted his eyes to heaven and prayed, saying:

6"You are the God who gives a reward to those who love You. Prepare yourself, my heart; rejoice and be glad in your tent, and say to your house of flesh, 'Your mourning has been turned into joy; for the Almighty is coming, and He will lift you up in your tent, for no sin has been found in you.'

7Take refreshment in your tent, in your virgin faith, and believe that you will live.

8Look at this basket of figs: they are sixty-six years old, and they have not withered or gone bad, but are dripping with milk.

9So my flesh will become for you, if you do what you were commanded by the angel of righteousness.

10He who kept the basket of figs will keep you again by His power."

11When Baruch had said this, he said to Abimelech, "Get up, and let us pray that the Lord will make known to us how we can send word to Jeremiah in Babylon about the shelter you were given on the way."

12Baruch prayed, saying, "Our strength, Lord God, the chosen light that came out of Your mouth,

13we beg and entreat Your goodness, great name that no one can know: hear the voice of Your servants, and let knowledge come into our hearts.

14What shall we do, and how shall we send this word to Jeremiah in Babylon?"

15While Baruch was still praying, an angel of the Lord came and said all these words to Baruch: "Counselor of the light, do not worry about how to send word to Jeremiah; for tomorrow at the hour of light an eagle will come to you, and you will reach Jeremiah.

16So write in the letter: Say to the sons of Israel: Let the stranger who has come among you be set apart, and let them keep fifteen days; after that I will bring you into your city, says the Lord.

17Whoever is not set apart from Babylon will not enter the city; and I will rebuke them, so that the Babylonians will not take them back again, says the Lord."

18When the angel had said this, he left Baruch.

19Baruch sent to the market of the Gentiles and got papyrus and ink, and wrote a letter that read: "Baruch the servant of God writes to Jeremiah in the captivity of Babylon:

20Rejoice and be glad, for God has not let us leave this body grieving for the city that was laid waste and outraged.

21For this reason the Lord has had compassion on our tears, and has remembered the covenant He made with our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

22He sent His angel to me, and he told me these words, which I have sent to you.

23These, then, are the words the Lord said, the God of Israel, who brought us out of the land of Egypt, out of the great furnace: Because you did not keep My ordinances, but your heart was lifted up and you stiffened your necks before Me, in anger and wrath I handed you over to the furnace in Babylon.

24So if you listen to My voice, says the Lord, from the mouth of Jeremiah My servant, whoever listens, I will bring him up out of Babylon; but whoever does not listen will become a stranger to Jerusalem and to Babylon.

25You will test them by the water of the Jordan; whoever does not listen will be made known. This is the sign of the great seal."

Notes

  • v6 "for the Almighty is coming" — ho hikanos, "the Sufficient One," the word the Greek of Ruth uses for Shaddai: the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me (Ruth 1:20).

  • v6 "Your mourning has been turned into joy" — Jeremiah's promise for the return, I will turn their mourning into joy (Jeremiah 31:13), here said by Baruch to his own heart.

  • vv6–10 "your tent… your house of flesh… So my flesh will become for you" — skēnōma, a tent, is the body, the dwelling of the heart. Baruch reads the figs as a sign: what kept them sixty-six years without decay will keep his flesh in the same way, and you will live (v7).

  • v16 "let them keep fifteen days" — the Ge'ez has fifteen too. In 9:1–2 the feast in Jerusalem runs nine days, and Jeremiah offers alone on the tenth.

  • vv16–17, 24 "Let the stranger who has come among you be set apart… whoever does not listen will become a stranger to Jerusalem and to Babylon" — the test of the return is separation from Babylon. Those who keep Babylon with them belong to neither city, and chapter 8 tells what became of them.

  • vv19–25 the letter — in the Ge'ez the main text stops where the letter begins; its editor printed the letter in a note, as a text with corrupt and missing words. The Greek gives it whole.

  • v23 "out of the land of Egypt, out of the great furnace… I handed you over to the furnace in Babylon" — Jeremiah's word for Egypt: out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace (Jeremiah 11:4). Babylon is a second furnace, and the God who brought them out of the first will bring them out of this one.

  • v25 "You will test them by the water of the Jordan" — as Gideon's men were sorted at the water: Take them down to the water, and I will refine them for you there (Judges 7:4).

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

chapters.title: The Eagle
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 7

1Baruch got up and went out of the tomb, and found the eagle sitting outside the tomb.

2The eagle spoke to him in a human voice and said, "Greetings, Baruch, steward of the faith."

3Baruch said to him, "You who speak are chosen from all the birds of the sky; that is plain from the brightness of your eyes. So show me: what are you doing here?"

4The eagle said to him, "I was sent here so that you may send through me any word you want."

5Baruch said to him, "Can you carry this word to Jeremiah in Babylon?"

6The eagle said to him, "That is what I was sent for."

7Baruch took the letter and fifteen figs from Abimelech's basket and tied them to the eagle's neck, and said to him, "I say to you, king of the birds: go in peace and in health, and bring me back word.

8Do not be like the raven that Noah sent out, which did not come back to him in the ark; be like the dove, which the third time brought word to the righteous man.

9So you too, carry this good word to Jeremiah and to those in chains with him, so that it may go well with you. Carry this papyrus to the people and to the chosen one of God.

10If all the birds of the sky surround you and want to fight you, fight back. The Lord give you strength.

11Do not turn aside to the right or to the left, but go straight like an arrow. Go in the power of God, and the glory of the Lord will be with you all the way you go."

12Then the eagle flew off with the letter on its neck and went to Babylon. When it arrived, it rested on a tree outside the city in a deserted place.

13It kept silent until Jeremiah came by, for he and some others of the people were going out to bury a dead man outside the city.

14Jeremiah had asked King Nebuchadnezzar, "Give me a place where I may bury the dead of my people," and the king had given it to him.

15As they went along weeping with the dead man, they came opposite the eagle.

16The eagle cried out with a loud voice, "I say to you, Jeremiah, chosen one of God: go and gather the people and come here, so that they may hear the letter I have brought you from Baruch and Abimelech."

17When Jeremiah heard this, he glorified God; he went and gathered the people, with the women and children, and came to where the eagle was.

18The eagle came down on the dead man, and he came back to life.

19This happened so that they would believe.

20All the people were amazed at what had happened, and said, "Is this not the God who appeared to our fathers in the wilderness through Moses, and now has appeared to us through this eagle?"

21The eagle said, "I say to you, Jeremiah: come, untie this letter and read it to the people." So he untied the letter and read it to the people.

22When the people heard it, they wept and put dust on their heads, and said to Jeremiah, "Save us, and tell us what to do so that we may enter our city again."

23Jeremiah answered them, "Keep everything you heard from the letter, and the Lord will bring us into our city."

24Jeremiah also wrote a letter to Baruch, saying: "My beloved son, do not be careless in your prayers, asking God for us, that He may prosper our way until we come out from under the decrees of this lawless king.

25For you were found righteous before God, and He did not let you come here, so that you would not see the affliction the Babylonians have brought on the people.

26It is like a father with an only son, when the son is handed over for punishment: those who see the father and comfort him cover his face, so that he will not see how his son is punished and be broken still more by grief.

27That is how God had mercy on you and did not let you come to Babylon, so that you would not see the affliction of the people.

28From the time we came here, grief has not left us: sixty-six years today.

29Often when I went out I found some of the people hanged by King Nebuchadnezzar, weeping and saying, 'Have mercy on us, god Zar!'

30When I heard this I grieved and wept a double weeping, not only because they were hanged, but because they were calling on a foreign god, saying, 'Have mercy on us.'

31I remembered the feast days we kept in Jerusalem before we were taken captive, and as I remembered I groaned, and went back to my house in pain and weeping.

32So now pray, in the place where you are, you and Abimelech, for this people, that they will listen to my voice and to the judgments of my mouth, and that we may go out from here.

33For I tell you, all the time we have spent here they have kept at us, saying, 'Sing us a song from the songs of Zion, the song of your God.'

34We say to them, 'How could we sing for you in a foreign land?'"

35After this Jeremiah tied the letter to the eagle's neck, saying, "Go in peace, and may the Lord watch over us both."

36The eagle flew off, came to Jerusalem and gave the letter to Baruch. He untied it and read it, kissed it, and wept when he heard of the griefs and afflictions of the people.

37Jeremiah took the figs and gave them out to the sick among the people, and he stayed on, teaching them to keep away from the pollutions of the nations of Babylon.

Notes

  • v8 "the raven that Noah sent out, which did not come back to him in the ark" — so the Greek of Genesis has it: the raven went out and did not return. The Hebrew says it went going out and returning, until the waters dried up (Genesis 8:7). The dove's third flight counts the raven as the first: the dove was sent twice after it, and came back the second time with an olive leaf, freshly plucked (8:11).

  • v11 "Do not turn aside to the right or to the left" — the words of the law, Do not turn aside to the right or to the left (Deuteronomy 5:32), given to a bird.

  • vv13–14 "going out to bury a dead man outside the city… Give me a place where I may bury the dead of my people" — the work Tobit did in Nineveh: if I saw any of my people dead and thrown out behind the wall of Nineveh, I buried him (Tobit 1:17).

  • vv18–20 "The eagle came down on the dead man, and he came back to life… Is this not the God who appeared to our fathers in the wilderness through Moses" — at Sinai God spoke of the exodus with the same bird: how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself (Exodus 19:4).

  • vv29–30 "Have mercy on us, god Zar!… they were calling on a foreign god" — no god of this name is known from Scripture. Zar is the Hebrew word for strange, foreign, as in the psalm, There shall be no strange god among you (Psalm 81:9), where the Hebrew is el zar; and v30 calls him a foreign god.

  • vv33–34 "Sing us a song from the songs of Zion… How could we sing for you in a foreign land?" — the psalm of the exile: "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!" How could we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land? (Psalm 137:3–4). The Greek has the psalm's words, pōs aisōmen… epi gēs allotrias.

  • v37 "Jeremiah took the figs and gave them out to the sick among the people" — the errand of 3:21, give them to the sick among the people, done at last, sixty-six years later and in Babylon.

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

chapters.title: At the Jordan
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 8

1The day came when the Lord brought the people out of Babylon.

2The Lord said to Jeremiah, "Get up, you and the people, and come to the Jordan, and say to the people: Whoever wants the Lord, let him leave behind the works of Babylon.

3As for the men who have taken wives from among them, and the women who have taken husbands from among them: let those who listen to you cross over, and take them up to Jerusalem; but those who do not listen to you, do not bring them there."

4Jeremiah spoke these words to the people, and they got up and came to the Jordan to cross.

5As he told them the words the Lord had spoken to him, half of those who had married among them would not listen to Jeremiah, but said to him, "We will never leave our wives; we will bring them back with us to our city."

6So they crossed the Jordan and came to Jerusalem.

7Jeremiah, Baruch and Abimelech stood and said, "No one who has joined with the Babylonians shall enter this city."

8They said to one another, "Let us get up and go back to Babylon, to our own place." So they went.

9When they arrived in Babylon, the Babylonians came out to meet them, saying, "You shall not enter our city, because you hated us and left us in secret; so you will not come in among us.

10For we have bound one another by an oath in the name of our god to take back neither you nor your children, since you left us in secret."

11When they learned this, they turned back and came to a deserted place far from Jerusalem, and built themselves a city, and called its name Samaria.

12Jeremiah sent to them, saying, "Repent, for the angel of righteousness is coming, and he will bring you into your high place."

Notes

  • vv2–3 "leave behind the works of Babylon… those who listen to you cross over" — the test the letter announced, You will test them by the water of the Jordan; whoever does not listen will be made known (6:25). The return is told as a second crossing of the Jordan.

  • vv3–5 "the men who have taken wives from among them… We will never leave our wives" — the question of Ezra's return: We have broken faith with our God and have married foreign women from the peoples of the land (Ezra 10:2). In Ezra the men agree to send the wives away (10:3); here half of them refuse.

  • vv6–8 "So they crossed the Jordan and came to Jerusalem… No one who has joined with the Babylonians shall enter this city" — those who would not leave their wives cross with them and come as far as the city, and are stopped at it by Jeremiah, Baruch and Abimelech.

  • vv9–10 "You shall not enter our city… to take back neither you nor your children" — the word of the letter kept: whoever does not listen will become a stranger to Jerusalem and to Babylon (6:24), and I will rebuke them, so that the Babylonians will not take them back again (6:17).

  • v11 "built themselves a city, and called its name Samaria" — the Ge'ez has the name too. The book gives its own account of where the Samaritans came from. Kings gives another: the king of Assyria settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the sons of Israel (2 Kings 17:24), people brought from other lands.

  • v12 "the angel of righteousness is coming, and he will bring you into your high place" — the angel Baruch named in his prayer (6:9). Your high place, ton topon hymōn ton hypsēlon, is not named: hypsēlos is used of a raised place on earth and of the height of heaven, and the sentence does not say which.

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

chapters.title: The Stone That Helped Jeremiah
chapters.html:
4 Baruch 9

1Those with Jeremiah stayed on, rejoicing and offering sacrifices for the people, for nine days.

2On the tenth, Jeremiah alone offered a sacrifice.

3He prayed, saying, "Holy, holy, holy, incense of the living trees, true light that gives me light until I am taken up to You:

4for Your mercy I plead; for the sweet voice of the two seraphim I plead; for another fragrance of incense.

5My meditation is Michael, the archangel of righteousness, who opens the gates to the righteous until he brings the righteous in.

6I plead with You, Lord Almighty of all creation, unbegotten and beyond understanding, in whom every judgment was hidden before these things came to be."

7As Jeremiah was saying this, standing at the altar with Baruch and Abimelech, he became like one who gives up his soul.

8Baruch and Abimelech stayed there weeping and crying out with a loud voice, "Woe to us, for our father Jeremiah, the priest of God, has left us and gone away!"

9All the people heard their weeping and ran to them, and they saw Jeremiah lying on the ground like a dead man.

10They tore their clothes, put dust on their heads and wept bitterly.

11After this they got ready to bury him.

12A voice came, saying, "Do not bury one who is still alive, for his soul is coming back into his body."

13When they heard the voice, they did not bury him, but stayed around his tent for three days, saying, "At what hour will he rise?"

14After three days his soul came back into his body, and he lifted up his voice among them all and said, "Glorify God with one voice! All of you, glorify God, and the Son of God who wakes us, Jesus the Messiah, the light of all the ages, the lamp that is never put out, the life of faith.

15After these times there will be another four hundred and seventy-seven years, and He comes to the earth.

16The tree of life that is planted in the middle of paradise will make all the fruitless trees bear fruit, and they will grow and put out shoots.

17The trees that have sprouted and boast, saying, 'We have lifted our tops into the air,' the firmly planted tree will make wither, with all the height of their branches, and will bring them to judgment.

18What is scarlet will become white as wool; the snow will turn black; the sweet waters will become salt, and the salt sweet, in the great light of the joy of God.

19He will bless the islands so that they bear fruit, by the word of the mouth of His Messiah.

20For He will come, and go out, and choose for Himself twelve apostles to preach the good news among the nations. I have seen Him adorned by His Father and coming into the world on the Mount of Olives; and He will fill the hungry souls."

21While Jeremiah was saying these things about the Son of God, that He is coming into the world, the people were angry and said, "These are the words spoken by Isaiah son of Amoz all over again, who said, 'I saw God and the Son of God.'

22Come, then: let us not kill him by that man's death, but stone him."

23Baruch and Abimelech were deeply grieved, because they wanted to hear in full the mysteries he had seen.

24Jeremiah said to them, "Be quiet and do not weep, for they will not kill me until I have told you everything I have seen."

25He said to them, "Bring me a stone here."

26He set it up and said, "Light of the ages, make this stone take on my likeness until I have told Baruch and Abimelech everything I have seen."

27Then by God's command the stone took on the likeness of Jeremiah.

28They stoned the stone, thinking it was Jeremiah.

29Jeremiah handed on all the mysteries he had seen to Baruch and Abimelech, and then he stood among the people, wanting to complete what was appointed for him.

30Then the stone cried out, "Foolish sons of Israel, why do you stone me, thinking I am Jeremiah? Jeremiah is standing among you."

31When they saw him, they ran at him at once with many stones, and what was appointed for him was completed.

32Baruch and Abimelech came and buried him, and they took the stone and set it on his tomb, writing on it: This is the stone that was Jeremiah's helper.

Notes

  • vv1–2 "for nine days. On the tenth" — the Ge'ez has the feast last seven days, and puts Jeremiah's sacrifice, as the Greek does, on the tenth day.

  • vv3–4 "Holy, holy, holy… the two seraphim" — the song of the seraphim in Isaiah's vision: Seraphim stood above Him… One called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts" (Isaiah 6:2–3). Isaiah does not give their number.

  • vv7–14 "lying on the ground like a dead man… for three days… his soul came back into his body" — Jeremiah lies as dead for three days, and the people wait to see at what hour he will rise. What he says when he rises is the book's last turn.

  • v14 "the Son of God who wakes us, Jesus the Messiah" — the Greek names Iēsoun Christon, and the Ge'ez also names Jesus, as the Messiah and the Son of God. From here to v20 the book speaks of His coming, His twelve apostles and the Mount of Olives.

  • v15 "another four hundred and seventy-seven years" — the Ge'ez gives another span, three hundred and three weeks of days.

  • v18 "What is scarlet will become white as wool" — Isaiah's promise, though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool (Isaiah 1:18), set among other things turned to their opposite.

  • v20 "He will fill the hungry souls" — the psalm: He… fills the hungry soul with good things (Psalm 107:9), where the Greek has the same words, psychēn peinōsan eneplēsen.

  • vv21–22 "I saw God and the Son of God… let us not kill him by that man's death" — Isaiah wrote, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne (Isaiah 6:1). The people hear Jeremiah saying what they blame Isaiah for saying, and they mean to kill him differently from the way Isaiah was killed, a death the book does not describe.

  • v32 "This is the stone that was Jeremiah's helper" — ho lithos ho boēthos, the name the Greek of Samuel gives Ebenezer: Lithos tou boēthou, "Stone of the Helper," where Samuel says, Till now the LORD has helped us (1 Samuel 7:12). Jeremiah's stone helped him finish what he had to tell.

  • Source text — Greek: Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, CC BY 4.0. Ge'ez: A. Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica (1866), public domain. English translation by this project.

speech.text: 4 Baruch 9
Those with Jeremiah stayed on, rejoicing and offering sacrifices for the people, for nine days.
On the tenth, Jeremiah alone offered a sacrifice.
He prayed, saying, "Holy, holy, holy, incense of the living trees, true light that gives me light until I am taken up to You:
for Your mercy I plead; for the sweet voice of the two seraphim I plead; for another fragrance of incense.
My meditation is Michael, the archangel of righteousness, who opens the gates to the righteous until he brings the righteous in.
I plead with You, Lord Almighty of all creation, unbegotten and beyond understanding, in whom every judgment was hidden before these things came to be."
As Jeremiah was saying this, standing at the altar with Baruch and Abimelech, he became like one who gives up his soul.
Baruch and Abimelech stayed there weeping and crying out with a loud voice, "Woe to us, for our father Jeremiah, the priest of God, has left us and gone away!"
All the people heard their weeping and ran to them, and they saw Jeremiah lying on the ground like a dead man.
They tore their clothes, put dust on their heads and wept bitterly.
After this they got ready to bury him.
A voice came, saying, "Do not bury one who is still alive, for his soul is coming back into his body."
When they heard the voice, they did not bury him, but stayed around his tent for three days, saying, "At what hour will he rise?"

After three days his soul came back into his body, and he lifted up his voice among them all and said, "Glorify God with one voice! All of you, glorify God, and the Son of God who wakes us, Jesus the Messiah, the light of all the ages, the lamp that is never put out, the life of faith.
After these times there will be another four hundred and seventy-seven years, and He comes to the earth.
The tree of life that is planted in the middle of paradise will make all the fruitless trees bear fruit, and they will grow and put out shoots.

The trees that have sprouted and boast, saying, 'We have lifted our tops into the air,' the firmly planted tree will make wither, with all the height of their branches, and will bring them to judgment.
What is scarlet will become white as wool; the snow will turn black; the sweet waters will become salt, and the salt sweet, in the great light of the joy of God.
He will bless the islands so that they bear fruit, by the word of the mouth of His Messiah.

For He will come, and go out, and choose for Himself twelve apostles to preach the good news among the nations. I have seen Him adorned by His Father and coming into the world on the Mount of Olives; and He will fill the hungry souls."

While Jeremiah was saying these things about the Son of God, that He is coming into the world, the people were angry and said, "These are the words spoken by Isaiah son of Amoz all over again, who said, 'I saw God and the Son of God.'
Come, then: let us not kill him by that man's death, but stone him."
Baruch and Abimelech were deeply grieved, because they wanted to hear in full the mysteries he had seen.
Jeremiah said to them, "Be quiet and do not weep, for they will not kill me until I have told you everything I have seen."
He said to them, "Bring me a stone here."
He set it up and said, "Light of the ages, make this stone take on my likeness until I have told Baruch and Abimelech everything I have seen."
Then by God's command the stone took on the likeness of Jeremiah.
They stoned the stone, thinking it was Jeremiah.
Jeremiah handed on all the mysteries he had seen to Baruch and Abimelech, and then he stood among the people, wanting to complete what was appointed for him.
Then the stone cried out, "Foolish sons of Israel, why do you stone me, thinking I am Jeremiah? Jeremiah is standing among you."
When they saw him, they ran at him at once with many stones, and what was appointed for him was completed.
Baruch and Abimelech came and buried him, and they took the stone and set it on his tomb, writing on it: This is the stone that was Jeremiah's helper.
